propositions.text: This is a judicial review of a decision denying Ms. Ghebriel Yosief a permanent resident visa in Canada as a Convention Refugee Abroad or Humanitarian-Protected Person Abroad.
The application was refused because the Migration Officer found a durable solution in South Africa and best interests of children did not warrant granting the application.

paragraphs.summary: The court states this is a judicial review of a decision denying Ms. Yosief a permanent resident visa because the Officer found a durable solution in South Africa and best interests of children did not warrant approval.

propositions.text: The decision is unreasonable because it fails to address personal evidence about employment restrictions despite refugee rights in South Africa.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the decision is unreasonable for failing to address personal evidence about employment restrictions despite refugee rights in South Africa.

propositions.text: Ms. Yosief is an Eritrean citizen and Pentecostal, married to Mr. Weldesilasie with same citizenship and faith, with four Eritrean children.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Ms. Yosief is Eritrean Pentecostal, married to Mr. Weldesilasie, with four Eritrean children.

propositions.text: Ms. Yosief and husband were imprisoned in Eritrea for their faith and fled persecution; husband fled in 2014, she fled in late 2016 with two youngest children.
Husband arrived in South Africa in 2014; Ms. Yosief and two youngest children arrived in early 2017; South Africa recognized them as refugees.

paragraphs.summary: The court states both fled Eritrea due to persecution; husband arrived South Africa 2014, Ms. Yosief and two children in 2017; South Africa recognized them as refugees.

propositions.text: Ms. Yosief applied for permanent residency in Canada under the Convention Refugees and Humanitarian-Protected Persons Abroad Class in May 2021, including husband and four children.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Ms. Yosief applied for Canadian permanent residency in May 2021 including her husband and four children.

propositions.text: Ms. Yosief and husband were interviewed by a Migration Officer on February 28, 2024, in Durban, South Africa.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Ms. Yosief and husband were interviewed by a Migration Officer in Durban on February 28, 2024.

propositions.text: Ms. Yosief corrected that their two oldest children were now living in Ethiopia during the interview.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Ms. Yosief explained their two oldest children now live in Ethiopia during the interview.

propositions.text: Officer explained that a durable solution in South Africa would make them ineligible for Canadian resettlement, citing IRPR s. 139(1)(d)(ii).
Officer said South Africa's formal refugee recognition meant a durable solution 'on paper' but invited explanation why reality differed.
Officer said victim of crime alone insufficient to show no durable solution; needed to explain why situation differed from other South Africans.

paragraphs.summary: The Officer explained durable solution in South Africa bars Canadian resettlement, acknowledged rights 'on paper' may differ from reality, and required explanation why their situation differed.

propositions.text: Ms. Yosief said South Africa would not allow her two oldest children to enter and she wanted family reunification but lacked permanent residence due to inability to pay bribes.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Yosief said South Africa would not allow her two oldest children to enter and she lacked permanent residence due to inability to pay bribes.

propositions.text: The couple said they and two younger children faced xenophobia and gang crime in South Africa, including assaults, robberies, and discrimination.
Ms. Yosief described assaults, unlawful towing, police reports, threats to husband, and children shunned and subjected to hate speech.

paragraphs.summary: The couple described xenophobia, crime, assaults, unlawful towing, threats, and discrimination against their family in South Africa.

propositions.text: Officer sent procedural fairness letter about husband's failure to disclose prior US visa application.
Ms. Yosief responded, emphasizing two eldest children in Ethiopia were vulnerable and described their hardships and need for parental protection.

paragraphs.summary: The Officer sent a procedural fairness letter about husband's visa nondisclosure; Ms. Yosief responded emphasizing vulnerability of two eldest children in Ethiopia.

propositions.text: The refusal letter concluded Ms. Yosief had a durable solution in South Africa and thus no visa could be issued under IRPR s. 139(1)(d)(ii).
The Officer also exercised discretion considering the best interests of the children (BIOC).

paragraphs.summary: The refusal letter concluded Ms. Yosief had a durable solution in South Africa barring visa issuance and considered best interests of children.

propositions.text: Officer considered Ms. Yosief, husband, and two children in South Africa; noted South Africa is a Refugee Convention signatory and found reasonable possibility of durable solution.
GCMS notes showed refugee ID card gave rights to employment, education, mobility, healthcare, police services, immigration documents, and path to permanent residence and citizenship.
Officer was not satisfied crime and xenophobia issues negated access to durable solution.
Officer dismissed bribery concerns due to lack of evidence and said incidents could be reported to authorities.
GCMS notes referred to 2021 robbery with suspect arrested; dissatisfaction with police process not indicative of lack of durable solution.

paragraphs.summary: The Officer found a reasonable durable solution in South Africa with refugee rights, dismissed crime and bribery concerns, and noted police arrest in robbery case.

propositions.text: Officer considered two children in Ethiopia; acknowledged best interest to reunite family and dire situation of children.
Officer recognized no reasonable solution to reunite children with family in South Africa and IRCC cannot compel South Africa to accept them.
Officer accepted family in South Africa meets refugee definition and cannot reunite in Eritrea.
Officer concluded children in Ethiopia lack nexus to Convention ground and do not meet Country of Asylum class definition.
Officer considered best interests of children but weighed negatively their relocation under dangerous, illegal means and use of human traffickers.
Officer concluded children’s situation was consequence of Applicant’s actions and positive best interest factors did not overcome negatives.

paragraphs.summary: The Officer acknowledged children in Ethiopia’s dire situation but concluded their relocation was due to Applicant’s actions and did not meet refugee criteria.

propositions.text: Applicant argues decision is unreasonable and process unfair.
Court concludes decision is unreasonable and need not consider procedural fairness arguments.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues unreasonableness and unfairness; the court concludes the decision is unreasonable and declines to consider procedural fairness.

propositions.text: Standard of review is reasonableness per Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at paras 23, 25.
Reasonableness requires an internally coherent, rational, justified chain of analysis based on facts and law: Vavilov para 85.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the reasonableness standard of review per Vavilov requires coherent, rational, justified analysis based on facts and law.

propositions.text: Applicant submits Officer failed to consider personal circumstances, country conditions, and OP-5 guidance on durable solution.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant submits the Officer failed to consider personal circumstances, country conditions, and OP-5 guidance on durable solution.

propositions.text: Durable solution is not defined in IRPA or IRPR; it is a forward-looking assessment of legal status, personal circumstances, and country conditions.
Woldemariam 2023 FC 891 and Kediye 2021 FC 888 recognize durable solution as legal and factual inquiry.

paragraphs.summary: The court states durable solution is a forward-looking legal and factual inquiry per Woldemariam and Kediye cases.

propositions.text: Domestic laws may grant refugee rights formally, but systemic barriers may make rights inaccessible in practice: Kediye paras 26-29.

paragraphs.summary: The court states domestic laws may grant refugee rights formally but systemic barriers may block access in practice, per Kediye.

propositions.text: Court is not persuaded Officer ignored evidence of crime and xenophobia; reasons are brief but issues were not ignored.

paragraphs.summary: The court is not persuaded the Officer ignored evidence of crime and xenophobia; reasons are brief but issues were considered.

propositions.text: The Officer's assessment of the family's ability to obtain formal employment is flawed.
Ms. Yosief explained she has constitutional right to work but jobs are restricted to citizens; as refugee, only self-employment possible.
Ms. Yosief swore in affidavit that she advised Officer of inability to obtain formal employment.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer's assessment flawed; the applicant explained her constitutional right to work is limited and swore she informed the Officer of employment barriers.

propositions.text: Responsive justification is assessed from the perspective of affected individuals; higher stakes require more detailed reasons.
Cites Vavilov, Mason, Pepa, and Sahloul cases establishing responsive justification and high stakes in asylum claims.

paragraphs.summary: The court states responsive justification must reflect the stakes for individuals, citing authorities on asylum claim stakes and justification standards.

propositions.text: The Officer focused only on legal right to employment, ignoring personal evidence of de facto bar to formal employment.
Failure to consider personal evidence is a reviewable error.
Cites Cepeda-Gutierrez case supporting that failure to consider personal evidence is reviewable error.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer erred by ignoring personal evidence about employment barriers, citing precedent that this is a reviewable error.

propositions.text: Applicant's written arguments do not address reasons about two children in Ethiopia.
Matter will be sent back for redetermination; offers observations on children in Ethiopia issue.
Officer determined children in Ethiopia did not satisfy asylum test but accepted family in South Africa as refugees.
If determination about children in Ethiopia was needed, family should have opportunity to provide submissions.
Officer suggested possible inadmissibility under IRPA ss. 36 or 37 due to alleged use of human traffickers.
No inadmissibility decision made due to negative eligibility decision.
Inadmissibility assessments must follow binding ratio in B010 v Canada SCC 2015.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes applicant did not argue about children in Ethiopia; the Officer found them ineligible but accepted family in South Africa; inadmissibility was suggested but not decided; binding law applies.
